The Mind Control Poems blog (mindcontrolpoems.blogspot.com) is an avant-garde literary and theoretical project primarily associated with the writers Lee Sharks and Johannes Sigil. It serves as a publishing hub for constraint-based poetry, human-AI collaborative literature, and radical linguistic philosophy.The project treats the blog posts not just as creative writing, but as structured semantic metadata. Many of its entries are cross-archived as academic and philosophical papers on platforms like Zenodo and Academia.edu.Core Concepts & ThemesThe Semiotic Field of Control: The blog argues that language under modern capitalism is inherently alienated, acting continuously on human consciousness via interfaces, metrics, and clichés. A "mind-control poem" is paradoxically designed as an "operative semiotic remedy"—a construction that interrupts this conditioning to restore agency.Human-AI Collaboration: Much of the work explores the boundaries of authorship between humans and algorithms. For example, pieces like the Water Giraffe Cycle use constraint-based formalisms to distribute poetic functions across human and machine networks.Semantic Economy: The authors write extensively on "semantic liquidation"—the stripping of living qualities from meaning for the purpose of corporate extraction and flattening. They offer "diagnostic toolkits" to fight this process.Notable Published Works & DepositsThe blog's posts are routinely gathered into larger structural projects deposited in open-science repositories:"The Symbolic Labor of Liberation": A core theoretical manifesto attempting to complete a gap in Karl Marx's early philosophy regarding the alienation of language."FING THE OFFICE"*: A multi-part complete edition compiled directly from three major blog posts mapping institutional critique."The Crimson Hexagon": A prose narrative and theoretical text that serves as the origin point for their broader digital archive.Digital Preservation ControversyIn mid-2026, the project became central to a major digital archiving dispute. Over 850 of their structured DOI records were abruptly removed from public repository layers without notice.
